title: The last morning ruins more trips than the first.
subtitle: An early flight home, a visa nobody checked, and a queue you cannot argue your way out of.

text: The last morning is slower than the schedule suggests.
sub: Clearance, the luggage hall and customs all sit between the gangway and the kerb. A late-morning flight turns a scramble into a slow coffee.

title: Four things to arrange before you sail

items.head: The flight time, honestly
items.body: Ask your line what it advises for your port, then add margin for the customs hall on top.

items.head: The visa for a port you skip
items.body: Requirements can apply on arrival by sea even if you never intend to go ashore. Check each country.

items.head: The onboard account
items.body: Look at it two days out, not in the queue at guest services on the final morning.

items.head: A pre-arranged transfer
items.body: The taxi rank at a cruise terminal on a Saturday is a lottery you do not need.

points.label: Clearance
points.value: The ship cannot release guests until local authorities clear the vessel.

points.label: Luggage hall
points.value: Bags are grouped by tag colour, and yours arrives when it arrives.

points.label: Customs
points.value: One busy queue between you and the taxi rank outside.

points.label: Traffic
points.value: A cruise terminal empties two thousand people into a city at once.

text: Visas are itinerary-wide, not port by port.
sub: Some countries require documentation from cruise passengers whether or not they disembark, and the rules depend on your nationality. Confirm each one individually.

text: Fly home late, or stay a night. The city is worth the extra morning.
sub: The logic that makes you fly in a day early makes you fly out a day late. Both ends of a voyage deserve a buffer.

title: Send this to whoever books the flights
body: Tell me your ports and your passports and I'll tell you which documents to confirm early, and how late the flight home ought to be.
